**Manifold Mesh Mix 1.6.0** rebuilds the CAD side of the converter. Mechanical parts now come out as the few clean faces a CAD program would make, not hundreds or thousands of small patches. Every conversion is measured against the mesh before it's saved. Messy meshes (coarse OpenSCAD exports, noisy scans, files with broken geometry) convert far better than before. On our 57-file test suite, **every file now converts to a valid solid that follows its mesh** (1.5.1: 45 of 57 followed the mesh, 56 were valid), with **47% fewer faces** in total.

Below is what changed, how each part works, and the measurements behind it.

## Downloads

- **macOS 14+ (Apple silicon):** `ManifoldMeshMix-1.6.0-macOS-arm64.zip`. Unzip it and drag the app into Applications. The app isn't notarized, so the first time you open it, right-click it and choose **Open**.
- **Windows 10/11 (64-bit):** `ManifoldMeshMix-1.6.0-Windows-x64-Setup.exe`. It installs just for your account, with no administrator password. If SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher, click **More info → Run anyway**.
- **Linux (x86-64):** `ManifoldMeshMix-1.6.0-Linux-x86_64.AppImage`. Make it executable and double-click it.
- Already have 1.0 or 1.5.1? Click the **⬇** button next to the app name; the app updates itself.
- `SHA256SUMS.txt` has the checksums. The apps check them when they update themselves.

## What's new

### 1. Every conversion is checked against the mesh

1.5.1 checked that a result was a valid solid with the right volume, and that the saved file read back fine. It never compared the shape with the mesh itself, so wrinkled, dented or saw-toothed results passed. 1.6.0 compares every result with its mesh the way you would by laying one over the other:

1. The shape is cut into fine triangles again, finer than the fit tolerance, from a copy written out and read back, so the check sees what a saved file holds.
2. Points are spread evenly over the mesh. For each one, the **exact distance** to the shape's surface is measured. Then the other way round, from the shape to the mesh, which catches extra material and flaps that no mesh point is near.
3. At every point, the **direction the surface faces** is compared with the mesh. Wrinkles and dents stay close to the mesh but tilt the surface, so they show up here even when the distances look fine.

A result **follows the mesh** when 99% of its surface is within 3 tolerances, 99.9% within 8 (so even a small flap or dent counts), and almost none faces the wrong way. The **File checked** badge shows how closely, for example "99.9% of the surface is within 0.13 mm of the mesh".

**Different meshes, different rules.** A clean CAD export, a coarse OpenSCAD model and a noisy scan can't be judged the same way. The engine measures each mesh first and picks its rules from those measurements:

- **Clean** (CAD exports, sculpts): the checks as described above.
- **Coarse** (an OpenSCAD 16-sided "circle", a low-detail export): a true curve stands off the mesh's flat triangles by up to the faceting, so the tolerance grows to match it, measured spot by spot.
- **Scan** (noisy): a smooth surface through the noise is right, so the tolerance grows to the noise. Single noisy points facing the wrong way don't count; only whole patches do.

**A certainty for every verdict.** A result near a limit, or with one spot further off than the mesh's coarseness explains (a notch or a rounded-off tip too small to move the percentages), gets a low certainty. Then a **second, finer check** decides. When the first method's result only just passes, **the other method runs too**, and the closer result is kept. The queue tells you when this happens (for example "Fitting smooth surfaces too (the first result only just passed)"), so you know why a file takes longer.

We also checked the checker itself. Its numbers were compared with exact calculations and with the saved files read back. Several of its own errors were found and fixed: coarse tessellation of some faces, an approximate nearest-triangle search, OpenCASCADE's meshing mistakes counted as gaps, and one edge far off its face hanging the mesher.

### 2. New CAD faces: swept surfaces and fillets

Before 1.6, anything that wasn't a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or torus became a patchwork of small freeform faces. Now the converter recognizes two more families of shapes:

- **Swept surfaces:** a profile moved along a path. That covers a straight pull (extrusions, straight gear teeth), a turn about an axis (revolved shapes), a screw motion (helical gear teeth, worm threads, tire treads) and a screw that also shrinks (tapered bevel-gear teeth).
  **How it works:** such a surface is unchanged by its motion, so every surface normal is square to the motion's velocity at that point. That gives one linear equation per mesh point, and the best motion is the smallest eigenvector of a 6×6 matrix (Pottmann & Randrup). How much better it fits than the next motion tells how sure the fit is. The points are then moved back along the motion into one plane, a smooth profile curve is fitted to them, and swept again. Small neighbouring pieces that lie on the same sweep join it.
- **Fillets along curved edges:** a rounded edge along a cam's outline, or where a pipe meets a sloping wall. These used to be cut into many small tori and cylinders. Now they're one pipe surface around a spine, measured from those pieces.

A new surface is only kept where it follows the mesh **no worse than what it replaces**, and simpler surfaces always win when they fit.

Results: a bevel gear went from 662 faces to 5, a planetary gear from 536 to 81, a small bevel gear part from 522 to 40, and a tapered boss from 32 to 4.

### 3. Clean borders between faces

Faces used to meet along **saw-tooth borders** that followed the mesh's triangles. That left jagged edges, faces that folded over themselves, and thin slivers that some slicers showed as bars or slits. Now:

- Jagged borders are **straightened** by a minimum cut through the triangles that fit both neighbouring surfaces, then **smoothed**.
- Slivers left behind join the surface they lie on. A border move that would leave a strip narrower than two tolerances is skipped.
- Edge curves are checked so they never fold back on themselves.

On the hub, mount and tire, this cut the number of saw-tooth edges from 154 to 48, 164 to 66 and 200 to 24.

### 4. Much better with bad meshes

- **Noisy scans** keep their real flat faces instead of falling apart into thousands of pieces, and slivers no longer punch holes in them.
- **Coarse exports** (few, long, thin triangles, typical of OpenSCAD) are judged by their own faceting. 1.5.1 misjudged how coarse they were at shallow creases and accepted surfaces that bulged between the mesh's points (a TPU liner's grooves were up to 1 mm off; now 0.01 mm).
- **The mesh check's hole fills never cut through the part.** Filling a big, uneven hole (the open back of a wheel, a car's window opening) with one patch could pass through the part behind it: on a car model, 13,087 of the 14,129 self-crossings reported were made by the fills themselves. Now each hole is filled on its own, only where the patch cuts through nothing, and the report says why any hole stays open.
- **Pieces touching along an edge each stay closed** when the mesh is repaired.
- **A freeform face that blows up** during fitting can no longer hang a conversion.

### 5. Files that are right in every program

STEP files don't keep everything OpenCASCADE keeps in memory. For example, per-edge tolerances are lost, so an edge saved with 0.1 mm reads back with 0.0000001 mm. A face that's valid in memory can therefore be broken in the saved file. 1.6.0 writes every face to STEP and reads it back **before** accepting the shape, and builds again any face that comes back broken. The finished file is still read back and checked after saving, as before.

### 6. Two versions when no method fits

If no method makes a shape that follows the mesh everywhere, the app keeps **both** the result closest to the mesh and a valid one. **Two versions were made** appears above the preview, and you pick: **Closest to the mesh** or the other version. The one you pick is shown and exported.

### 7. Preview, progress and small fixes

- **Faces OpenCASCADE can't mesh** no longer show up as holes or slits in the STEP preview. They are remeshed at other settings until they're covered, using a precise area measurement to tell when.
- **Live progress:** while a file is read and checked, the queue and preview show each step ("Looking for hidden internal walls", "Filling holes", …) with a progress bar. During conversion they show each method being tried and each second check.
- **3MF projects with many touching parts:** the question about touching parts listed every name, which could push the buttons off the screen. It now lists the first 8 and "and N more".
- Dark specks where faces meet in the preview are gone.
- Bug reports include the engine build, how closely the result follows the mesh, and which of two versions you picked.

## Measured on the whole test suite

57 files: generated test models (`tests/make_models.py`: CAD parts, messy meshes, scans, organic shapes), public gear and mechanism models (planetary gearbox, worm gearbox, bevel gears) and users' problem files. Both versions were run with Auto at the same quality on the same computer. Accuracy was measured with 1.6.0's checker on the saved STEP files of both versions.

| | 1.5.1 | 1.6.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Valid solids | 56 of 57 | **57 of 57** |
| Follow the mesh | 45 of 57 | **57 of 57** |
| Faces, all files together | 27,947 | **14,707** (−47%) |
| Time, all files together | 54 min | 72 min (+32%) |

Selected files (largest gap between the STEP and the mesh, in mm):

| File | 1.5.1 | 1.6.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Printed hub (user file) | 2,243 smooth patches, 2.84 mm ✗ | **214 CAD faces, 0.08 mm** |
| Headrest mount (user file) | 2,156 smooth patches, 1.52 mm ✗ | **182 CAD faces, 0.07 mm** |
| Tractor tire (user file) | 1,186 faces, 0.32 mm | **610 faces, 0.12 mm** |
| TPU liner (user file) | 102 faces, 1.04 mm ✗ | **93 faces, 0.01 mm** |
| Noisy scanned plate | 443 smooth patches, 0.72 mm ✗ | **13 CAD faces, 0.05 mm** |
| Filleted bracket | 64 faces, 0.99 mm | **56 faces, 0.04 mm** |
| Shelled enclosure | 56 faces, 0.61 mm ✗ | **52 faces, 0.03 mm** |
| Bevel gear | 662 faces, 0.05 mm | **5 faces, 0.04 mm** |
| Planetary ring gear | 2,184 smooth patches, 1.24 mm ✗ | **1,255 CAD faces, 0.17 mm** |
| Planetary carrier | 1,032 faces, **not a valid solid** | **594 faces, valid**, 0.11 mm |
| Planetary planet gear | 536 faces, 0.02 mm | **81 faces, 0.01 mm** |
| Worm gearbox case | 66 faces, 0.98 mm ✗ | **70 faces, 0.04 mm** |
| Complex mechanism part | 2,558 mixed patches, 0.96 mm ✗ | **1,780 CAD faces, 0.05 mm** |

✗ = doesn't follow the mesh by the rules above.

## Known problems and limits in 1.6.0

- **Slower conversions.** CAD is tried first on more parts, and results are checked more thoroughly. The whole suite takes about a third longer. Simple parts that took 2 seconds now take 4–20. Some of the biggest files are faster, because fewer faces need building.
- **One small flap on a very complex part:** on one complex test part with about 1,800 faces, a spot about 0.16 mm off the mesh is left (it still passes the checks). Faces built in the converter's last rounds aren't measured against the mesh yet; that's next.
- **Slits in some slicers:** a few faces may show thin slits in slicers that use OpenCASCADE to mesh STEP files, even though the STEP file is valid and reads back correctly. The app's own preview works around this; slicers don't.
- **Smooth and scanned shapes** (for example a scanned lamp cover) can still come out as hundreds of small patches. A cleaner layout for those is planned.
- **Very complex lattices** (like the gyroid test model) take 25 minutes or more and can still come out with face errors.

If you find a file that converts badly, please [open an issue](https://github.com/TUNA-THE-FIRST/Manifold-Mesh-Mix/issues) and attach the report from **Save Report…**.
